hook_clip: Here's how to reverse engineer BambooHR from a written spec. Claude passed all twenty checks, but my spec never said not to email the new hire whose offer fell through.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: We gave Claude one Markdown file. It copies the part of BambooHR a small team needs so onboarding stops slipping. A template turns a start date into dated tasks. Each task has one owner: the manager, IT, the people team, a buddy, or the new hire. Late tasks are flagged, and everyone gets one email a day with what's theirs.

The core rule is due dates. Every task is due a set number of days before or after the start date. If that lands on a weekend, it moves to the Friday before. So for a Monday start, the desk task, one day before, is due on Friday. And when the start date moves, every open task moves with it.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation, with templates, people and sign-in. Onboardings and tasks. The new hire's view. Then the daily job, the digests and the export. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser, from fresh seed data.

Here's what it built. Priya Nair's onboarding shows her manager, her buddy, and Ben's laptop task, due a week before she starts. The onboardings list shows Leo Grant with two tasks overdue. Creating one for Rosa warns that four tasks are already overdue, because her start date is close. Ben's tasks are grouped by when they're due. And Leo's first weeks shows what others are doing for him, by first name only.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all twenty checks passed, along with one hundred and nine automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The build exposed forty-four gaps in the spec. Places where Claude had to guess. Check-in notes were private, yet any role could own a check-in, so the wrong person could end up reading one. Nothing stopped the people team from deactivating themselves. And a task title starting with an equals sign could run as a formula in the export. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't the same as production-ready. We didn't test production sign-in, real email delivery, the hourly job on a real scheduler, other time zones, or hosting. Those are yours to check before your team relies on it.

So is it worth building? BambooHR charges a flat two hundred and fifty dollars a month for Core, up to twenty-five employees. Above that, it starts at ten dollars and twenty-five cents per employee per month. But that buys a whole HR system. If you need records, time off, payroll and benefits, buy it. If onboarding is the part you need, build it.
Everything is in one file. The data model, thirteen rules, seed data, four phase prompts, and all twenty checks, with the forty-four fixes already in.
